formNote: Most scholars read a flower’s calyx; the Shuowen reads a bird flying up toward the sky (一) and not coming down. Either way, “not” is a sound loan.
summary: The everyday negator of Chinese, borrowed for its sound. Joined with 二 it forms 不二, “not two” — the Chinese rendering of Sanskrit advaya.
placement: In the eye of the left wing — one of the two equilibria the trajectory circles forever without ever reaching.

satellites.title: Calyx, or Rising Bird
satellites.evidence: Two readings of the earliest graph: a calyx with drooping sepals (the majority view; the original sense was later written 柎), or — with the Shuowen — a bird soaring to the sky line and not returning.
gaps: Name a modern palaeographic source for the calyx reading.

satellites.title: The Eight Negations
satellites.evidence: Kumārajīva’s Nāgārjuna opens with eight negations — 不生亦不滅，不常亦不斷，不一亦不異，不來亦不出 — rendering Sanskrit privatives such as an-utpāda, “non-arising”. Such negation denies without asserting the opposite.
satellites.caveat: The technical name for this, prasajya-pratiṣedha (“non-implicative negation”), comes from later commentators such as Bhāviveka, applied back to Nāgārjuna.
gaps: Cite a source for Bhāviveka and prasajya-pratiṣedha.

satellites.title: Two Readings, One Tone Shift
satellites.evidence: bù, the ordinary negator, rises to bú before a falling tone — so 不二 is said bú èr. A second reading, fǒu, “or not; to deny”, survives in classical usage, a sense also written 否.

satellites.title: Negating Deeds vs. Things
satellites.evidence: Malay splits negation by what is negated: tidak negates verbs and adjectives, bukan negates nouns and whole propositions — much as Classical Chinese uses 不 for verbal and 非 for nominal predicates.
